name: Eclipse Zenoh
vendor: Eclipse Foundation; developed mainly by ZettaScale Technology
summary: A pub/sub, query and storage protocol that runs peer to peer or through routers, from microcontrollers to the cloud; also a ROS 2 middleware.
intro: Zenoh names data by key, a path such as `myhome/kitchen/temp`, and offers three things on keys. Publishers `put` values that every matching subscriber receives. A `get` sends a query to every queryable whose key expression matches, and wildcards such as `myhome/**` work on both sides. Storages are queryables that remember the latest value for each key they cover. Applications link a library: the reference implementation is in Rust, with bindings for C, C++, Python, Kotlin, Java, Go and TypeScript, plus zenoh-pico, a separate pure-C implementation for microcontrollers. In peer mode, the default, applications find each other on the local network by multicast scouting and talk directly, with no broker. In client mode a constrained device keeps a single session to a router, `zenohd`, and routers link sites together. Routers load plugins: a storage manager with backends such as memory or S3, a REST API on port 8000, and an MQTT plugin that acts as a broker for MQTT 3 and 5 clients.

Zenoh is an incubating Eclipse Foundation project, dual-licensed under EPL 2.0 and Apache 2.0, and free to use. Its main developer and sponsor is ZettaScale Technology, founded in 2022, which sells support and a commercial Zetta Platform. Zenoh 1.0 shipped in October 2024 with a stabilised API, and its ROS 2 middleware, `rmw_zenoh`, became a Tier 1 option alongside the DDS implementations in ROS 2 Kilted Kaiju (May 2025).
strengths: Pub/sub and queries on the same keys, so a dashboard can ask for the latest values and then subscribe to changes with one library
Peer to peer on a local network: two devices next to each other talk directly instead of through a remote broker
Scales down to microcontrollers with zenoh-pico; the project quotes a wire overhead of 4 to 6 bytes
A Tier 1 ROS 2 middleware since Kilted Kaiju, and plugins bridge MQTT and DDS systems into the same network
limits: A much smaller ecosystem than MQTT or Kafka: one main implementation, mostly from one company, and no cloud provider offers it as a managed service
Storages keep the latest value per key, not a replayable log; history needs a backend such as a database
Its own protocol: MQTT clients and DDS applications only join through plugins or bridges
The API changed substantially before 1.0, with a migration guide from 0.11, and the project is still incubating at Eclipse
With `rmw_zenoh`, ROS 2 nodes need a Zenoh router running to discover each other, because multicast discovery is off by default

sections.title: A router that stores what it sees
sections.intro: The `zenohd` configuration behind the snippet. The storage subscribes to `myhome/**` and answers queries for it; the REST plugin lets you read the same data with `curl http://localhost:8000/myhome/**`.

sections.title: Zenoh or MQTT?
sections.intro: Both carry small messages from devices on topics or keys. They differ in topology, in what they store, and in how many implementations exist.

values: Peer to peer, client to router, or a mix, chosen per application

story: Angelo Corsaro, then CTO of PrismTech and co-chair of the OMG group behind the Data Distribution Service (DDS) standard, worked on very large distributed systems for military, aerospace and smart-city projects. He saw no single protocol that covered them end to end. DDS handled pub/sub well but, in his view, could not scale up to the internet or down to microcontrollers; CoAP was client/server; and MQTT made two devices on the same network talk through a remote broker. Nothing let you query data at rest without knowing where it lived.

Zenoh set out to cover all of it with one protocol: pub/sub, geo-distributed queries and storage, from microcontroller to data centre, in any topology. In 2020 the team brought it to the Eclipse Foundation and rewrote the router in Rust; the first Rust-based release, Aithusa, came out in October 2020 with DDS and ROS 2 integration. ZettaScale was founded in 2022 to develop it commercially.

Its biggest step came from robotics. In September 2023 the ROS 2 core team published a report choosing a non-DDS middleware to build a new RMW on, which became `rmw_zenoh`. Zenoh 1.0 followed in October 2024, and `rmw_zenoh` became Tier 1 in ROS 2 Kilted Kaiju in May 2025.

choices.choice: Peer to peer first, routers optional
choices.why: Sending traffic between two machines on the same network through a cloud broker adds latency and a single point of failure. Peers discover each other by multicast and talk directly; routers are added only where sessions must be shared or networks joined.

choices.choice: Queries and storage in the protocol
choices.why: Pub/sub alone only covers data in motion. Making queryables and storages first-class means an application can ask for data at rest by key without knowing which database holds it.

choices.choice: A Rust core with a separate C version for microcontrollers
choices.why: The 2020 rewrite put the router and main library in Rust, with other languages as bindings, while zenoh-pico reimplements the protocol in plain C for devices too small for the Rust stack.
